title: From Past to Present: The Roles of Attachment and Social Support in Buffering Lifetime Adversity and Intergenerational Trauma
abstract: Abstract Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) predict greater adulthood adversity and offspring trauma exposure. Nurturing relationships (for example, with friends, family members, and romantic partners) have been shown to protect against negative health outcomes of ACEs during adulthood, but less is known regarding their capacity to buffer continuity in adversity over the lifespan and across generations. The current study examined whether adult attachment security and social support moderated the associations between a parent’s history of ACEs, adulthood adversity, and children’s early adversity. Data were drawn from a longitudinal study of early social-emotional development in a socioeconomically diverse community sample ( N = 205 parent-child dyads; parents 94.1% female, 69.3% White/non-Hispanic; 14.2% at or below federal poverty line). At T1 (children aged 1–2 years), parents self-reported their ACE history, completed a semi-structured interview on social support, and participated in a story stem task assessing attachment security. At T2 (children aged 3–4 years), parents reported on recent adversity and their child’s exposure to adversity. Findings showed parental ACEs were positively associated with adulthood adversity and children’s early adversity. Social support significantly moderated these associations, rendering them non-significant at above-average levels of support. Planned follow-up analyses revealed similar patterns for emotional and instrumental support, although instrumental support did not significantly buffer the association between parental ACEs and children’s early adversity. Attachment security did not moderate any of the examined associations. Findings suggest that enhancing social support may be a promising strategy for preventionefforts designed to disrupt continuity of adversity and foster parent-child dyad well-being.
